hypothesis.title: The Precursor Field
hypothesis.question: Do listeners perceive identical musical target events differently when only the three-second approach field changes?
hypothesis.hypothesis: If a fixed musical target is preceded by different three-second precursor fields that vary accessibility, prosodic contour, and hidden-source cues, then listeners will rate the same target as more prepared, blocked, surprising, or inevitable depending on the precursor field rather than the target itself.
hypothesis.rationaleMd: S3 reports that severe stuttering events can carry detectable prosodic precursors in a three-second audio window, suggesting that short pre-event acoustic fields can encode upcoming disruption. S6 separates relatively static timbral identity from dynamic hierarchical prosody, supporting a test where the identity of the target stays fixed while the approach contour changes. S2 adds a path-accessibility model: systems may move to the nearest accessible metastable state rather than the globally optimal one. S5 supplies a harmonic version of accessibility through Tonnetz/combinatorial neighborhood structures. S1 warns, by analogy, that premature measurement/collapse can destroy coherent joint possibility, while S4 frames hidden/off-screen causes as meaningful audio-generation targets. Together these sources support treating the pre-arrival region as a compositional control surface rather than incidental lead-in.

recipe.title: Three Seconds Before Arrival
recipe.bodyMd: Write a sixteen-bar loop with four fixed target events: one cadence, one timbral bloom, one rhythmic break, and one sudden silence. Render five versions in which the targets remain identical but the three seconds before each target change. Version A uses nearest-neighbor Tonnetz-like voice leading and gradual timbral/rhythmic movement toward the arrival [S5, S2]. Version B uses hard two-beat or two-note block resets, echoing the collapsed-block constraint in the HHL music architecture [S1]. Version C exaggerates subtle prosodic precursor cues over the three-second window: tempo drag, energy-envelope tilt, pitch-contour narrowing, spectral-flux increase, or breath-like noise [S3]. Version D adds acousmatic/off-screen cues that imply a hidden cause, such as room tone swelling, distant friction, or preparatory vocal noise [S4]. Version E keeps timbral identity constant while changing only dynamic prosody: articulation, contour, timing, and intensity [S6]. Blind-listen to the renders and rate the identical target arrivals for preparation, surprise, blockage, inevitability, and emotional coherence.
dawChecklist: Create a 16-bar loop at 96 BPM with four clearly marked target arrivals.
Duplicate the session into five render lanes or project versions.
Keep the target-event audio/MIDI identical across all versions.
Edit only the three seconds before each target in each version.
Render accessible-path, collapsed-block, prosodic-warning, hidden-cause, and identity/prosody-split versions.
Randomize filenames before listening so the condition is hidden.
Rate each fixed target on preparation, surprise, blockage, inevitability, and emotional coherence.
Compare whether ratings change despite identical targets. If not, reject or revise the precursor-field design.

protocol.listeningContext: studio headphones or monitors, blind randomized render order
protocol.listeningMethod: rate each identical target arrival after one full pass and one focused pass around each three-second window
whatVaries: dynamic contour while timbre stays fixed
whatStaysConstant: mix level of the target events

notes: Disconfirming evidence: if blinded ratings do not change across conditions despite altered precursor fields, then the current three-second approach design is not perceptually load-bearing.
